note:
Hosea introduces his prophecy, naming himself as God’s messenger. His name means “salvation.”

**Uzziah ... Jeroboam.** Whereas four kings of Judah are named—Uzziah (also called Azariah, 767–740 B.C.), Jotham (750–735 B.C.), Ahaz (735–715 B.C.), and Hezekiah (715–686 B.C.)—the only northern king recorded is Jeroboam II (c. 793–753 B.C.). Perhaps Hosea thinks that the northern kings who reigned between Jeroboam II and the fall of the north in 722 (four were assassinated) are not worthy of mention.

Hosea’s experience duplicates the Lord’s experience. The prophet will learn the bitter taste of betrayal just as the Lord himself has (Introduction: Special Issues). On the theme of marital and covenantal unfaithfulness, see Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

**the land commits great whoredom.** All the inhabitants of the land are deemed unfaithful, like Hosea’s wife.

Her name has no symbolic significance, unlike the names of her children.

**him.** This pronoun is omitted in vv. 6, 8, but its absence does not necessarily imply that Hosea is not the father there also, since the indirect object may be implied.

Lit. “God sows” or “God plants.” This is the name of a beautiful and fertile valley between the mountain ranges of Samaria and Galilee (the site of Gideon’s victory over the Midianites; cf. Judg. 6:33), and of a town at the valley’s southern end, where Jehu came to power through violence (1 Kin. 21:1; 2 Kin. 9; 10). This valley becomes the place of judgment in 733 B.C. (2 Kin. 15:29). This punishment through military defeat suggests the theme of covenant breaking since it reflects the curses recorded in Lev. 26:17; Deut. 28:25, 49–57. Yet Jezreel is also a sign of blessing and fertility in Hos. 2:22.

**the house of Jehu.** King Jeroboam II of Israel is from the house of Jehu, a dynasty established through a bloodbath at Jezreel (2 Kin. 9:14–37; cf. 1 Kin. 19:16, 17) and ending with the murder of Zechariah (2 Kin. 15:8–10).

Israel’s military strength, symbolized by the bow (Gen. 49:24; 1 Sam. 2:4; Ezek. 39:3), is finally broken by the Assyrian army under Tiglath-pileser III, who conquers the northern territories of Israel.
Hb. _Lo-ruhama_, lit. “she has not received mercy.” The child’s name signifies the imminent withdrawal of the compassion God has shown to Israel in spite of the nation’s covenant unfaithfulness.
A prophecy of Jerusalem’s miraculous deliverance from the Assyrians in 701 B.C. (Is. 37:14, 33–38; 2 Kin. 19:32–37).

Hb. _Lo-ammi_. The name of the third child marks the extremity of God’s judgment, as God cancels the ancient covenantal formula (Ex. 6:7; Lev. 26:12; Deut. 26:17–19) and declares that the covenant is no longer in in effect (v. 10 notes).

**I am not your God.** Lit. “I am not ‘I AM’ to you,’’ a reference to the divine name for God used in Ex. 3:14.

The increasingly severe prophecies of judgment symbolized in the names of the three children are now dramatically reversed.

**1:10 sand of the sea.** A clear reference to the ancient patriarchal promise of innumerable descendants (Gen. 22:17; 32:12; cf. Gen. 13:16; 15:5; 26:24; 28:14).

**You are not my people.** The promise of restoration to these people is fulfilled at least in part when remnants of the north are later joined with the south during the reign of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 30:11, 18) and after the exile (1 Chr. 9:3; Ezra 8:35). The NT applies this promise to the church, the true Israel, composed of both Jews and Gentiles (Rom. 9:24–26; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10). For the apostles, the remnant of ethnic Israel was evidently a model for the remnant of the nations: what applied to the former applied to the latter.

**Children of the living God.** This unique expression suggests the kind of intimate relationship God desires with Israel, one in which God gives life (as opposed to the lifeless relationship Israel has with Baal). In Is. 40:18–20; 44:9–20; 46:5–11, dead idols are contrasted with the living God. The living relationship is now provided in Jesus Christ (Matt. 16:16; Rom. 9:26).

This reveals the completeness of reconciliation between both kingdoms and the Lord. Ultimately, this reunion takes place under Christ, the son of David (Matt. 1:23; 2:6, 15).

**they shall go up from the land.** Israel’s restoration begins in the return from exile. The phrase may also refer to resurrection from death (Ps. 71:20; Is. 43:6).

**the day of Jezreel.** See note on 1:4.
Hostile siblings Israel and Judah will be fully reconciled, and the horrible indictments contained in the names “Lo-ammi” (1:9 note) and “Lo-ruhama” (1:6 note) will be reversed.

God brings a case against Israel in which the children are to accuse their mother.

**she put away.** Repentance and reconciliation are the final goals of God’s judgment (vv. 9–23).

If repentance does not take place, the unfaithful wife (Gomer/Israel) will be publicly exposed (v. 10) and left destitute, traditional punishments for an adulteress (Ezek. 16:37–39; Nah. 3:5–7), though less severe than the death penalty (Deut. 22:22).
See 1:2. God’s love and mercy (1:6) will also be withdrawn from the children who, like their mother, are charged with promiscuity.

verse_quote: their mother has played the whore.
note: The unfaithful mother (Israel) has looked to Canaanite fertility religion and not to the Lord (v. 8) to provide the staples of life.

The woman’s initiative, representing all Israel, is stressed.

**my first husband.** The early period of intimacy in reference to the Lord is remembered fondly (cf. 11:1–4).

verse_quote: grain, the wine ... silver and gold.
note: Israel has credited the Lord’s agricultural and commercial gifts (Deut. 7:13; 11:14; 28:1–12) to Baal. In texts discovered at the ancient north Syrian city of Ugarit, Baal is seen as the god of the storm and worshiped as the provider of rain and fertility.

Though not punished with death (v. 3 note; cf. Ezek. 16:37–40), the unfaithful and forgetful lover is severely chastised through a series of dramatic reversals in which God’s gifts are withdrawn: failed harvests, exposure, and the end of festivals.

**2:9 take back.** The Hebrew indicates a forceful, snatching action.

The Hb. word translated as “Sabbath” (_shabbat_) is derived from the verb meaning “stop” or “cease,” making a sarcastic pun with “put an end to” regarding the Sabbaths.

**appointed feasts.** The festivals have become occasions for religious syncretism in which the worship of the Lord and Baal are intermingled. See Introduction: Occasion.
The prostitute’s wages, which are in fact gifts from the Lord (v. 8), are to be destroyed.

On pagan goddesses in the region, jewelry emphasizes the erotic areas of the anatomy. A tie between idolatry and jewelry is made in Gen. 35:4.

**her lovers.** In vv. 7, 10, 12 these are probably synonymous with the Baals. The essence of the charge against Israel is that she has forgotten the Lord, whom she should love (cf. 4:6; 13:4–6). See theological note “Syncretism.”

There Israel is to love God alone (v. 16; cf. Jer. 2:2).

**speak tenderly to her.** Lit. “speak to the heart,” an idiom used elsewhere for wooing, speaking kindly, and coaxing (Gen. 34:3; Judg. 19:3; Ruth 2:13).

Lit. “Valley of Trouble,” this area is near Jericho and is the site of the stoning of Achan (Josh. 7:24–26). Though associated with sin and death, this valley is to be transformed into a “door of hope.”

The Hb. word _baal_ can mean “master” or “husband” and can also refer to the pagan god Baal. Israel’s use of the noun _baal_ in reference to the Lord blurs the distinction between the two. In the future, Israel will be so zealous to stamp out anything associated with Baal worship that the word _baal_ itself, in all its senses, will be avoided (v. 17).

verse_quote: I will make for them a covenant.
note:
Taking up the same theme in a later era, Jeremiah explains the covenant as entailing a new heart (Jer. 31:31–34).

**with the beasts.** In Hosea’s day, wild animals are a threat, particularly after invading armies ravage the land, but the future kingdom will be secure and peaceful, free from the threat of wild animals (Is. 11:6–9) and invasions (Ps. 46:9; Is. 2:4; Mic. 4:3). The language may be figurative for a transformed humanity, with the resulting peace and security attending the renewal to be consummated at Christ’s return.

Betrothal is the final step in the courtship process and involves paying a bride-price to the bride’s father. Here the qualities of righteousness, justice, love, mercy, and faithfulness are a sort of bride price that guarantees the permanence of the relationship.

**righteousness.** God’s righteousness is expressed both in His fairness and in the salvation He bestows on His people (10:12; Amos 5:7).

**justice.** This term can denote the legal decisions and relationships by which justice and fairness are established and restored (5:11; 6:5; 10:4; Amos 5:15, 24; Mic. 6:8).

**steadfast love.** See note on Ex. 15:13; 34:6.

**mercy.** The term can refer to compassion, heartfelt sensitivity, and love (1:6; Gen. 43:14; Deut. 13:17; 2 Sam. 24:14).

This quality includes dependability, truthfulness, and steadfastness in one’s relationships (Ps. 88:11; 89:1, 2, 5, 8, 24; 92:2; 98:3). Christ, by His active obedience, provides these covenant virtues for His people. By the Holy Spirit He inscribes His own nature on their hearts (2 Cor. 3:3).

**know.** The essence of the new covenant relationship involves knowing the Lord intimately (Jer. 31:34). Today Christ mediates this new covenant and renders the old covenant relationship obsolete (Heb. 8:7–13).

The Lord will graciously answer Israel’s cry as she learns again to answer His appeals (v. 15).

**the heavens.** The Lord will show that He, not the storm-god Baal, commands the cycles of nature whereby the land becomes fertile and produces the crops that were earlier withheld (v. 9). See Introduction: Occasion.
See note on 1:4, in which Jezreel is a sign of curse, in contrast to its function as a sign of blessing here.

The promises of restoration come to a climax as Jezreel is redeemed (v. 22; cf. 1:4, 5), Lo-ruhama (1:6 note), is shown God’s love and Lo-ammi (1:9 note) becomes God’s people.

**I will sow.** This is a wordplay on the name “Jezreel.”

**You are my God.** See Rom. 9:23–26 and 1 Pet. 2:9, 10 regarding the fulfillment of these promises.

Hosea recounts his reconciliation with his wife Gomer as an anticipation of God’s reconciliation with Israel.

**3:1 love ... even as the Lord loves.** God’s apparently unreasonable request to Hosea is patterned after His own loyal, protective, and bountiful love for undeserving Israel.

**cakes of raisins.** These delicacies, made from raisins pressed together, are associated with special occasions (2 Sam. 6:19), and may serve in Baal worship as an aphrodisiac (cf. Song 2:5).

An act of redemption on Hosea’s part. Christ similarly fulfilled this picture of love in action when He redeemed His saints from the slave market of sin.

**shekels.** The payment, roughly half in silver and half in produce, amounts to about thirty shekels and approximates the price of a slave in Ex. 21:32. The NT teaches that Christ’s blood is the cost of redemption from the penalty of death (1 Pet. 1:18).

The waiting period until the coming of Christ, the great and final King of the Davidic dynasty (v. 5).

**without king ... household gods.** Israel’s basic political and religious institutions, both legitimate (sacrifice and ephod; Ex. 28:31) and illegitimate (sacred stones or pillars and idols or teraphim; Deut. 16:21, 22; Zech. 10:2), are going to be removed as punishment.

Many Israelites later repent with a full desire for intimacy with God, such as the Jews who repent at Pentecost (Acts 2:38–41).

**David.** This reference points to Jesus Christ, Son of David (1:11 note; cf. 2 Sam. 7:12–16; Matt. 1:1; Rom. 1:3).

**the latter days.** A reference to the period extending from the first coming of Christ until His second coming and beyond. See note on Mic. 4:1.

In this striking example of a prophetic lawsuit against Israel for violating the terms of the covenant, Hosea gives an overview of the Lord’s case against Israel and then focuses on the consequences of the nation’s rejection of the knowledge of God.

**4:1 faithfulness ... knowledge.** See notes on 2:19, 20.
These sins constitute violations of the foundational covenant document—the Decalogue (Ex. 20:2–17; Deut. 5:6–21). Five of the commands of the Decalogue are listed here.
Human sin results in crises within the natural order that endanger all of life (Lev. 18:28; Is. 24:4, 5).

Attention shifts to the sins of the priests, whose failure to instruct the nation in God’s law has corrupted Israel (v. 6; cf. Deut. 31:9–13; 33:10).

**4:4 let no one contend.** Or, “let no man bring a charge.” According to the Mosaic law, the priests are entrusted with the task of rendering legal judgments (Deut. 17:9–13). But because of the general lack of knowledge and respect for God’s law in Israel during Hosea’s time, there is no point in bringing charges against another because the verdicts will not be honored (the people are “like those who contend with the priest” [text note]; i.e., they do not respect his decisions and teaching).
The nation of Israel (2:2, 5; Is. 50:1).

The nation will lose her covenant relationship with God through lack of covenant knowledge (vv. 8, 12).

**knowledge.** Knowledge of God is inseparable from the law of God (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). The priests, who are responsible for teaching the law, and their descendants are to be punished for ignoring or forgetting the law (vv. 4–10 note).

Or, “they will change their glory.” Ultimately, the Lord is Israel’s glory (Is. 60:19; Jer. 2:11). In Rom. 1:23, Paul condemns the sin of exchanging God’s glory for something corruptible.

**shame.** Idols or false gods (Deut. 32:16, 17).

verse_quote: They feed on the sin of my people.
note: In a literal sense, the priests, who eat portions of the animals sacrificed for sin (Lev. 6:26), encourage the people to sin so that they will have more to eat. In a figurative sense, the priests are gratified by the people’s sin.
No one is spared from judgment (cf. Is. 24:1–3). People naturally follow their religious leaders for good or ill.
Food will not satisfy (v. 8), and illicit sex will not produce increase. They have left the Lord, the source of life, to practice harlotry (vv. 12, 18; 2:4; 6:10; 9:1), just as Gomer has done.
Lit. “take away the [people’s] heart,” i.e., their ability to judge and think clearly (cf. Prov. 31:4, 5).

Lit. “their wood.” This may refer to the Asherah pole beside a Canaanite shrine (Deut. 16:21; Judg. 6:25–32), to some other deity (Hab. 2:18, 19), or to a sacred tree thought to give oracles (Judg. 9:37).

**staff.** Probably a divining rod, or perhaps a small figurine of Asherah.

**spirit of whoredom.** Their spiritual adultery is caused by an intoxicating and seductive power that draws them continuously into sin (cf. “spirit of confusion” in Is. 19:14; “spirit of deep sleep” in Is. 29:10).

It is not that God refuses to punish the harlots and adulteresses at all (since the people as a whole will be judged), but that He will not allow them to be punished while the men who patronize them go free (cf. Gen. 38:24–26).

The theme of prophetic lawsuit against Israel continues as further charges of covenant disobedience are leveled (4:1–19 note).

**4:15 Gilgal.** This important Israelite sanctuary near Jericho is situated across the Jordan from Baal-peor. Gilgal was the first place Israel camped during the settlement under Joshua. From the time of the conquest, Gilgal has been an important place of worship (Josh. 4:19–5:12; 1 Sam. 10:8; 11:12–15). Later in Israel’s history, Gilgal becomes associated with wicked and syncretistic religious practices (9:15; 12:11; Amos 4:4).

**Beth-aven.** Lit. “house of wickedness” or “house of deception.” This is a contemptuous nickname for Bethel (“House of God”)—a royal, but apostate, sanctuary for the northern kingdom (1 Kin. 12:28–33; Amos 4:4; 5:5; 7:13). One of Jeroboam’s calves was located here (1 Kin. 12:29).

**As the LORD lives.** This orthodox oath (Judg. 8:19; Ruth 3:13; 1 Sam. 14:39) is forbidden here because they are lying (v. 2), or because it is being misused by linking the Lord to Baal worship. The Lord’s name is not to be associated with the practices of those sites.
The Israelites are kicking against all of the Lord’s efforts to care for them (cf. Jer. 31:18).

Because Ephraim is by far the largest and most centrally located of the ten northern tribes, the northern kingdom of Israel is sometimes called Ephraim (Deut. 33:17 note). From the time of Joseph to the time of Samuel, Ephraim was expected to be the tribe that provided leadership for Israel.

**leave him alone.** The plural verb here may indicate an address to other prophets or to other Israelites.

A wordplay on the Hb. word meaning “wind” or “spirit” is probably intended. Not only is a destructive storm wind of divine judgment about to sweep away the people (Job 1:19), but also “the spirit of whoredom” (v. 12; 5:4) is leading them to ruin. The Israelites are caught up in a gale of idolatry.

verse_quote: priests ... house of Israel ... house of the king.
note:
The fate of the northern kingdom is bound up with that of its leaders. The priests are responsible to teach the law (4:6), and the royal house is responsible for administering justice.

**snare.** The leaders have trapped their foolish subjects.

**Mizpah.** Probably the Mizpah in Gilead where Jeph­thah was made ruler and a syncretism between the gods of Ammon and the Lord prevailed (Judg. 10:17; 11:8–33).

**Tabor.** A famous mountain site located on the northeastern edge of the Jezreel Valley (Judg. 4:6). These and other northern sites have become high places of the pagan cult of Baal in Hosea’s day.
See note on 4:17.
See note on 4:12. They “know not the Lord” truly (4:1, 6), nor can they return or repent (cf. Jer. 13:23).
The sins of the people testify against them in the Lord’s covenant lawsuit against His people (4:1–19 note).
They will not find the Lord through the offering of their ritual sacrifices (4:13; 1 Sam. 15:21–23; Is. 1:11–17; Mic. 6:6–8).

Like an unfaithful wife and mother, Israel is giving birth to children who are literally and religiously illegitimate (4:6, 13, 14).

**new moon.** The festivals bring judgment instead of the Lord’s blessing on their wombs and crops as they have imagined would happen (cf. Is. 1:13, 14).

These commands sound the watchman’s cry to warn of an approaching enemy (Judah) from the south (cf. 8:1). The Syro-Ephraimite war described in 2 Kin. 16:5–9 and 2 Chr. 28:5–21 seems to be the context behind this warning. See Introduction: Occasion.

**Gibeah ... Ramah ... Beth-aven.** These Benjaminite towns lie in a straight line running north from Jerusalem: Gibeah, three miles (5 km); Ramah, five miles (8 km); Beth-aven (Bethel), eleven miles (17 km). At various times in their history, they are claimed by one kingdom or the other (1 Kin. 15:16–22).
The boundaries separating family property are marked by stones (Deut. 19:14; 27:17; Job 24:2; Prov. 22:28; 23:10). See note on Num. 27:1–11.

Like a moth, or possibly like an infection (some suggest that the Hb. word translated “moth” means “pus”), God will bring inexorable and unpleasant decay upon sinful Ephraim and Judah. A moth eats garments, and dry rot destroys the timbers of a building.

Instead of turning to the Lord for healing from their miseries inflicted by an enemy (cf. Is. 1:5–9; Jer. 30:12, 13), Israel has turned to Assyria. Assyrian records speak of the tribute paid by two of Israel’s kings, Menahem and Hoshea (cf. 2 Kin. 15:17–20; 17:3).

verse_quote: I will be like a lion.
note: Even with Assyrian help, Israel and Judah are helpless prey before the powerful lion, the Lord (13:7; Amos 1:2; 3:8).
In His anger, God removes His saving presence from the people until they truly repent (3:5).

The response of this song of repentance echoes the imagery of 5:11–14. The prophet includes himself in this call to repentance, so there is yet opportunity for restoration.

**6:1 let us.** The priests may be quoted here, much as Israel was quoted in 2:7.

**return.** The call to return to the Lord is one of the central messages of the book (2:7; 3:5; 5:4, 15). True repentance and conversion bring reconciliation that includes healing of wounds (cf. Deut. 32:39).

This may simply denote a short period of time. Some, who view this as a prediction of Christ’s resurrection, understand Paul to allude to this verse in 1 Cor. 15:4.

**live before him.** See Ps. 16:11.

verse_quote: press on to know the Lord.
note:
Like the call to return (v. 1), the call to true knowledge of the Lord is central to Hosea’s message (2:8, 20; 4:1, 6; 5:4; 6:6). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

**as the dawn ... as the showers.** These similes compare God’s reliability to the recurrent events of nature that revive.
Continuing the use of images from nature, God laments the temporary, transitory quality of Israel and Judah’s covenant love in contrast to His own faithfulness (v. 3).

Like the light of the sun whose rising dispels the darkness and dries up the dew, God’s justice consistently and inevitably goes forth (cf. Ps. 37:6), exposing the sins of those who have broken the covenant.
Covenant faithfulness or loyalty, not mere ritual, is required of the covenant people (Mic. 6:6–8 and notes).

These verses catalog a number of crimes associated with specific places that are infamous in Hosea’s day. Though the details are now lost, the record serves to indict the whole nation (v. 10).

**6:7 like Adam.** Several possible interpretations of this reference have been proposed: (1) the first man, Adam (Gen. 3); (2) a place identified with the ancient site Tell ed-Damiyeh on the Jordan River (Josh. 3:16), paralleling Gilead and Shechem (vv. 8, 9) and suggested by “there” in the second half of the verse; and (3) humanity. Because the elements of a covenant were present in God’s relationship with Adam, the doctrine of God’s covenant with Adam does not depend upon the interpretation of this text. See note on Gen. 3:1-24.

This is a mountainous region in the northern Transjordan, but the word may refer to the city of Ramoth-gilead.

**evildoers.** The term is used frequently in the Psalms to indicate the enemies of the righteous and of the Lord.

**tracked with blood.** This may allude to the fifty men of Gilead involved in the assassination of Pekahiah (2 Kin. 15:25).
An important religious and political center, Shechem is located in Ephraimite territory between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal (Deut. 27:4, 12–14; Josh. 8:30; 20:7; 24:1; Judg. 9:6; 1 Kin. 12:1).

The phrase suggests a religious sin or the involvement of priests or prophets in gross wrongdoing (Jer. 5:30, 31; 18:13–15; 23:14).

**whoredom.** A common figure here for religious infidelity (7:4 and note).
A metaphor for God’s judgment (Jer. 51:33; Joel 3:13; Matt. 13:39–43).
Both terms refer to the northern kingdom, of which Samaria is the capital (4:17 note). The Lord’s grace shines a light on Israel’s sins.
They have deceived even themselves (cf. Gal. 6:7).
The royal leaders should provide moral leadership, but they have savored instead the evil and treachery of those around them (2 Kin. 15:8–30).

They have left the Lord, to whom they were allied in the covenant, and have joined themselves with other gods and other foreign allies (2:4; 4:12–14; Jer. 9:2; 23:10–14). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

**like a heated oven.** The figures of an oven, a baker, and fire present a graphic word picture of the self-propagating passion, treachery, and wickedness that infests the political life of Israel during its last days and leads to the series of violent assassinations of its kings (2 Kin. 15:8–30). The assassination of Pekah by Hoshea (2 Kin. 15:30) may be the occasion of the remarks in vv. 4–7.
A royal celebration becomes an occasion for drunkenness, which in turn fuels more wickedness (1 Kin. 16:9, 10; Prov. 31:4, 5; Amos 6:6).
Those plotting against the king, perhaps the priests (6:9).
Even amid unrest that has seen four kings assassinated within twenty years (2 Kin. 15:8–30), none of the leaders have called upon God.

A reference to Israel’s shifting alliances with Egypt, Philistia, Aram, and Assyria.

**a cake not turned.** In this sarcastic figure for foolish national policy, Israel is compared to a useless half-baked cake that cannot be eaten because she has refused to turn to the Lord.

They have made Ephraim poor by exacting tribute.

**he knows it not.** This repeated phrase stresses Israel’s ignorance of how politically weak and drained she has become. Lack of knowledge of God is here followed by a lack of self-knowledge and by self-deception.
Israel’s blindness is attributed to stubborn arrogance that testifies against her (5:5). Turning back to the Lord is Israel’s only hope (2:7; 3:5; 5:4; 6:1; Amos 4:6–12).

In Hosea’s era, the dove is reputed to be witless and easy to trap.

**Egypt ... Assyria.** Like a dove, Israel has fluttered from one nation to another seeking security and protection: Menahem submitted to Assyria and paid a vast tribute (2 Kin. 15:17–20); Pekah formed a coalition with Syria-Damascus against Assyria (2 Kin. 15:29, 37; 16:5); and Hoshea shifted his allegiance from Assyria to Egypt (2 Kin. 17:3, 4).
The Lord’s net of judgment will come down upon flitting Israel.

This term from commercial law meaning “buy back” (Lev. 27:27–31) is used also of Israel’s deliverance from bondage (13:14; cf. Ex. 13:15; Deut. 7:8; 9:26; 15:15; Mic. 6:4).

**lies.** This may refer to the false ideas about the Lord that has been imported into Israel’s religion, to insincere words of repentance (6:1–3), or more generally to the broken promises of the covenant.

A responsible and loyal response, as suggested by a similar expression used in a contemporary Assyrian treaty.

**wail upon their beds.** This phrase could mean that they cry out to their gods on the beds of fertility-cult prostitution.

**gash themselves.** Cutting oneself is a pagan Canaanite ritual to cause Baal to intervene in one’s behalf (1 Kin. 18:26–29).

See Ps. 78:57.

**insolence of their tongue.** These are directed against God and His prophets (6:5).

**Egypt.** The Egyptians will soon mock at the fall of those who have solicited their help only intermittently.

The urgent call for alarm (5:8) indicates that Assyria, like an eagle or vulture, is rapidly approaching to administer God’s judgment.

**the house of the** LORD**.** The temple in Jerusalem is at the very heart of the land of God’s people.

**my covenant ... my law.** Rebellion against the terms of the covenant is tantamount to rebellion against God Himself (4:6; 6:6, 7; 7:13; 8:12).
As they cry for help, the Israelites claim to know God, but their actions belie their words (6:1). They truly do not know the Lord (5:4).
This comprehensive term describes all the blessings under God’s covenant. It may even refer to the “Good One,” God Himself (Amos 5:14, 15; Mic. 6:8).

Israel’s independence from God in the political sphere is apparent in her refusal to consult God in her choice of leaders. This leads to a series of conspiracies and violent assassinations (7:3–7; cf. 2 Kin. 15:8–30).

**idols.** In making gods of silver and gold, Israel expresses her defiant rejection of God (v. 5; cf. Ex. 20:3–6; 34:17; Lev. 19:4).
A symbol of fertility and strength, the bull was frequently worshiped in the ancient Near East and is itself here described as the object of worship (10:5 note).

verse_quote: sow the wind ... reap the whirlwind.
note: This proverbial saying emphasizes the dire cause-and-effect relationship between sin and punishment (10:13; cf. Job 4:8; Prov. 11:18; 22:8; Gal. 6:7–9).

Probably a reference to Hoshea’s submission to Assyria in his attempt to keep the power that he seized following his murder of Pekah (7:11; cf. 2 Kin. 15:30; 17:3).

**wild donkey.** Using a wordplay between the Hb. for “wild donkey” and the Hb. name _Ephraim_, Hosea condemns Ephraim (Israel) for stubbornly rejecting the Lord’s company.

This gathering is for judgment, not restoration (Joel 3:2; Zeph. 3:8).

**the king and princes.** The king of Assyria (Is. 10:8).
Although built to atone for sin, northern altars instead have become places to sin.
God threatens them with captivity, here symbolized by the land where Israel was once enslaved (9:3; cf. Ex. 1:8–14; Deut. 28:68).

Israel’s confidence that buildings and fortifications bring spiritual, political, or military security is misguided.

**fire.** See Amos 1:4, 7, 10, 12, 14.

Because of divine judgment on her covenant disobedience, Israel will not enjoy the fruit of the land (Deut. 28:18), nor will she celebrate the annual agricultural feasts (Deut. 16:1–17 and notes).

**9:1 threshing floors.** The flat, open area used for threshing wheat and barley is also a place where Israel has prostituted herself by indulging in sensual activities related to the fertility worship of Baal.
This device is used for both wine and oil.

LORD**.** Also called the Lord’s “house” (8:1; 9:15), the Promised Land is owned by the Lord and not by Baal—or even by Israel (Lev. 25:23 and note). Exile from this land is another consequence of Israel’s idolatry.

**return to Egypt.** See note on 8:13.

**unclean food.** Other nations and the food they produce are considered unclean (Ezek. 4:13; Amos 7:17).

Food in the house of mourners is unclean because of contact with a dead body (Num. 19:11–22; Deut. 26:14).

**house of the** LORD**.** They will be unable to sanctify their food through sacrifice while in exile.
. A probable reference to the annual fall harvest Feast of Booths or Tabernacles (Lev. 23:33–43; Deut. 16:13–15).

The Assyrian invasions.

**Memphis shall bury them.** Here poetically paired with Egypt, this Egyptian city is known for its great cemeteries, tombs, and pyramids.

**precious things of silver ... tents.** The abandoned tents and valuables may be religious shrines and idols, or their personal property in general.

In their sin, the Israelites have considered the Lord’s prophets to be foolish and idle talkers.

**man of the spirit.** Used in parallel with “prophet,” this is probably another expression for “man of God” (1 Sam. 10:6; 1 Kin. 18:12; 22:21–28; 2 Kin. 2:9, 16).

**mad.** The Hb. word indicates a nonsensical babbler or madman (1 Sam. 21:13–15; 2 Kin. 9:11; Jer. 29:26).

The prophets keep watch over Israel (5:8; cf. Jer. 6:1; Ezek. 3:17; 33:1–7). But the one who has sounded the alarm now finds himself hunted like an animal and an object of hostility.

**the house of his God.** The temple (8:1 note).

A town infamous for the gang rape of the Levite’s concubine and the war that followed (Judg. 19–21). The gravity of Israel’s former sins also shows how deeply they require a complete renewal of their nature.

An unusual and delicious find.

**first fruit on the fig tree.** The early fig that ripens on the previous year’s sprouts is not only very tender but quite uncommon (cf. Is. 28:4). These images stress how exceptional and pleasing was the Lord’s initial covenant relationship with Israel.

**Baal-peor.** A reference to Israel’s sexual and spiritual adultery in the wilderness (Num. 25 and notes)—behavior that is paralleled by Hosea’s contemporaries.

**became detestable.** By joining themselves to Baal-peor, the god of shame, the Israelites themselves became detestable.

Possibly her political and military power, but the context suggests that it is her large population. The blessing on Joseph and Ephraim had made them fruitful (Gen. 48:16; 49:22–26).

**no birth.** The practice of fertility religion generates a fertility curse, not a blessing (Deut. 28:18).

Hosea responds in prayer, asking that God’s fertility blessings be withdrawn (Gen. 49:25; Ex. 23:26; Deut. 28:4, 11). The prophet can only agree with God’s righteous judgment. Israel has sought fertility from Baal, but Hosea prays that the God of Israel will answer with infertility.

See note on 4:15; cf. 12:11.

**drive them out of my house.** Although the emphasis here is upon expulsion from the temple, this punishment parallels God’s banishment of the Canaanites (Ex. 23:29, 30; 33:2; Josh. 24:18; Judg. 6:9). See note on 8:1.

“Ephraim” sounds like “fruit” in Hebrew, and the wordplay ironically underscores the tragedy of Ephraim’s fruitlessness (Gen. 41:52). The name of this leading northern tribe is often used in Scripture for the entire northern kingdom of Israel.

Unlike the people who have turned away from God, the prophet has remained faithful to the covenant.

**wanderers.** Having wandered from God (7:13), the Israelites, like Cain, are destined to be exiled, with no true home (Deut. 28:64, 65).

In this section, unlike in the preceding and following sections, the Lord does not speak, but the prophet speaks about Him.

**10:1 more his fruit increased ... more altars he built.** Israel has given the credit for prosperity to their idols, and they have devoted more resources to the pagan cult whenever their prosperity has increased.
The covenant requires single-minded devotion to the Lord (Deut. 6:5); Israel’s divided loyalties call forth the judgment predicted in the covenant curses pronounced by Moses (Deut. 29:14–29).
Whether the king is still on the throne and about to be deposed, or he has already been deposed, he is useless without God’s blessing.
Or “wormwood,” as the Hb. term is translated in Amos 6:12.

The capital city of the northern kingdom.

**calf of Beth-aven.** The calf and its priests (2 Kin. 23:5; Zeph. 1:4) are probably not representative of a foreign deity. Rather, they exemplify a highly perverse form of worshiping the Lord in Israel (cf. 8:5 note; 13:2 note; 1 Kin. 12:31–33). This is likely a reference to the calf of Bethel erected by Jeroboam I (cf. 4:15).

**mourn.** Hosea mocks the pious emotions that the people manifest for an idol.

See 4:13–15.

**Cover us ... Fall on us.** The words speak of overwhelming devastation from the Lord. The people would rather die than face further judgments from Him. The passage is quoted by Jesus in Luke 23:30, and it is alluded to in Rev. 6:16.
See note on 9:9.
May refer to the past sin at Gibeah and the present sin of Israel, to Israel’s religious sin and political faithlessness, or simply to Israel’s repeated and unyielding transgressions.

Both kingdoms are in view.

**trained calf ... loved to thresh.** A positive image of Israel’s original calling as a teachable animal without a muzzle and free to eat as it threshes the harvested grain because it willingly does what it is told (11:4; cf. Deut. 25:4; Prov. 12:10; Jer. 50:11).

**fair neck.** That is, a strong neck capable of arduous work. Israel has not fulfilled the Lord’s expectations. The easy yoke of covenant blessings will be replaced by the hard yoke of covenant curses in order to teach them obedience.

See note on Ex. 15:13. Sowing what is right and good brings a harvest of blessing from the Lord. Here is another call to repentance from the prophet.

**break up your fallow ground.** When virgin and fallow ground is plowed, it produces a particularly abundant harvest.

**rain righteousness.** God must give the harvest (1 Cor. 3:6, 7).

Instead of cultivating a fruitful relationship with God, Israel has planted, reaped, and eaten wickedness and dishonesty (8:7; Gal. 6:7–9).

**Because you have trusted in ... your warriors.** The punishment God will bring (a military defeat) is directly related to Israel’s sin of depending on its own military power and not on the Lord (Jer. 9:23, 24).

Hosea’s original audience must remember this now-unknown event as particularly brutal. Shalman is an unknown figure. He has been identified variously as Shalmaneser III of Assyria (859–824 B.C..), Shalmaneser V (727–722 B.C..), and Salamanu, a contemporary Moabite king. Beth-arbel is often identified with the site of Irbid in Gilead.

Often ironically called “Beth-aven” by Hosea (4:15 note; 5:8; 10:5).

**At dawn.** The time for battle to begin.

In language as tender as the story of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32), God, the loving parent, proclaims His compassion for Israel. In spite of rebellion, God’s election cannot be defeated. Beyond judgment there is hope.

**11:1 loved.** The language of love is used to describe both the father-son relationship and the covenantal relationship between a suzerain and vassal in ancient Near-Eastern treaties (Deut. 6:5; 7:8, 13; 10:15; 23:5).

**out of Egypt I called my son.** Here and in v. 4, reference is made to God’s deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt (Ex. 4:22). Jesus, as the true Israel, was also brought out of Egypt (Matt. 2:15).

verse_quote: they were called ... they went away.
note: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult to translate. The meaning may be that the pagans or their gods, the Baals, have tempted Israel, causing the nation to depart from the Lord. Alternatively, those who are called may be the prophets, whose messages are ignored as Israel went after other gods.

Probably a reference to God’s tender leading of Israel through the wilderness to the Promised Land as a father leads a little child.

**I healed them.** God spared Israel from harm during the formative wilderness period (Ex. 15:26).
The imagery apparently returns to Israel as a work animal (10:11), but here God is pampering the creature by easing the yoke and reins on it.

The Hb. word for “not” here seems to indicate that Israel will not return to Egypt (symbolic for bondage; cf. 8:13 note), but such a reading appears to conflict with 8:13; 9:3; and 11:11. Some render this phrase as a rhetorical question (“shall he not return?”), while others emend the Hb. word for “not” to mean “to it.” Another reading, however, is indicated by the context of divine mercy in this passage (vv. 4, 8). Israel shall not return to Egypt (i.e., to her status before God called her as His covenant people, Deut. 4:34), but she will be punished for her sins by Assyria. In other words, she will not return to the oppression of Pharaoh but will come under the oppression of the king of Assyria.

**Egypt ... Assyria.** See notes on 8:13; 9:3. Though deserved, the effect of this judgment is tempered in v. 11.

With fortified cities they are self-reliant (8:14).

**gates.** Some suggest that this difficult Hb. word refers to people, specifically to false prophets who supplied the military counsel mentioned later in the verse.

verse_quote: How can I give you up.
note:
Here God is speaking directly to Israel. The contrast with vv. 5–7 heightens the impact of this deeply personal declaration of relentless compassion.

**Admah ... Zeboiim.** These two cities on the plain near the southern end of the Dead Sea (Gen. 10:19; 14:2, 8) were destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:23–25), thus becoming examples of God’s wrath (Deut. 29:23; Jer. 49:18).
Holiness denotes God’s moral perfection. Men seek revenge, but God works salvation.
LORD**.** Restoration, not destruction, is the goal of God’s judgment of His covenant people.

God compassionately tempers the effect of the judgment pronounced in v. 5. Although the people have breached the Mosaic covenant and deserve to experience its curses without mitigation, God promises that they will be restored to the land.

**from Egypt ... Assyria.** Again Egypt and Assyria are paired to symbolize the judgment of God’s people through exile (8:13 note; 9:3; 11:5).

This section accuses Israel of betrayal and pronounces judgment. Recurrent themes are the past treachery of Israel (artistically linked with episodes from the life of Jacob) and the rejection of the word of the Lord as spoken by the prophets.

**11:12 surrounded me with lies.** The northern kingdom lacks integrity before God.

**Judah still walks with God.** The Hebrew is difficult to translate. As rendered here, Judah is viewed positively and contrasted with Ephraim (i.e., Israel). But some translate the phrase to speak of Judah as “unruly against God,” and thus like Ephraim.

See Prov. 15:14; Is. 44:20.

**wind ... east wind.** These images of futility (Job 15:2; Eccl. 1:14) and destruction (13:15; cf. Jer. 18:17) are applied to Israel’s alliances with Assyria (5:13; 7:11; 8:9; 14:3; cf. 2 Kin. 17:3) and Egypt (7:16 note; cf. 2 Kin. 17:4). Such alliances are not merely poor foreign policy but expressions of faithlessness against the Lord.

**falsehood.** Examples of deception include Israel’s vacillation between Assyria and Egypt (7:11), and playing off the latter against the former (2 Kin. 17:3, 4).

**oil.** Gifts are often given when making covenants.

As in 4:1, the Lord acts as plaintiff, judge, and prosecutor in a court scene, bringing a covenant lawsuit against His people. He calls for punishment (v. 2) but also reconciliation (v. 6).

**Jacob.** That is, Israel (10:11; cf. Gen. 32:28).
The Hebrew here is the root for “Jacob” (Gen. 25:26) and is translated “cheated” in Gen. 27:36.

The Hb. root for “strive” is given as the source of the name “Israel” in Gen. 32:28. In tenaciously seeking God’s blessing, Jacob set a positive example for the nation (v. 6).

**Bethel.** The place where God made Himself known to Jacob (Gen. 28:12–19; 35:1–15). See note on 4:15.

LORD**, the God of hosts.** A doxology, similar to those in Amos (Amos 4:13; 5:8, 9; 9:5, 6), here reminds Israel that the covenant God of the patriarchs (the Lord) is the God of hosts, the commander of Israel’s armies, and sovereign over all creation (Zech. 1:3 note).

**memorial name.** See Ex. 3:15.
Like Jacob, who returned to Bethel to fulfill his vow (Gen. 35:1–15), Israel must return to the Lord.
The merchant Ephraim has been dishonest and cruel.

verse_quote: I am the LORD your God ... Egypt.
note:
The statement is one of self-presentation. It introduces the following expression of God’s will to His covenant people (Ex. 20:2; Deut. 5:6).

**tents ... appointed feast.** A reference to the Feast of Booths, when the people live in booths in memory of Israel’s time in the wilderness after leaving Egypt (Lev. 23:43). Just as Israel was judged with forty years of wilderness wandering (Num. 14:33), here Israel is threatened with the “wilderness” of exile from the land.

No one can plead ignorance as an excuse (6:5; 12:13).

**visions.** A mode of revelation to the prophets (Num. 12:6; Job 33:14–16).

**parables.** These “parables” are figures of speech bearing divine messages (2 Sam. 12:1–4; Ps. 78:2; Is. 5:1–7; Ezek. 17:2–10).

This region east of the Jordan, bordered by Moab on the south and Bashan on the north, is a place of illegal sacrifices, bloodshed, and idolatry. It is conquered by Assyria in 734–732 B.C.. (6:8; cf. 2 Kin. 15:29).

**Gilgal.** See note on 4:15.

**heaps on the furrows.** Large stones struck by the farmer’s plow are piled in heaps.

Paddan-aram (Gen. 28:2, 5).

**served ... guarded.** Hosea compares Jacob’s service to secure a wife from a foreign country with God’s rescue of His people from Egypt.

The first prophet is clearly Moses (Deut. 18:15; 34:10–12) and the second probably is as well. The preserving prophet could, however, be a later prophet such as Samuel (Jer. 15:1) or Elijah (1 Kin. 19:9–18).

Again God’s covenant faithfulness (v. 13) is contrasted with Israel’s faithlessness. The Lord has been provoked by the worship of pagan gods (Deut. 32:21), but here even more offenses seem involved.

**bloodguilt.** A reference either to murder itself (4:2; 5:2; 6:8) or, as in ancient legal texts, to any capital crime. The verse concludes the lawsuit, and is parallel in structure to v. 2, which introduces the section. Covenant election entails covenant responsibility.

This begins an announcement of judgment for sins past (v. 1) and present (v. 2).

**Ephraim.** See note on 4:17.

**Baal.** See 2:7, 8, 17; 9:10; 11:2.

**died.** Because of its idolatry, the northern kingdom (Ephraim) is regarded as spiritually dead and lifeless.

The collective picture is of small statues of calves molded of bronze and overlaid with silver (Ex. 32:4, 8; 34:17; Lev. 19:4; Deut. 19:16). The calf idol is Canaanite and linked with Baal worship, but the idolaters probably also associate it in their own minds with the Lord (8:5, 6; 10:5 and notes).

**kiss.** An act of devotion, adoration, or appeasement (1 Kin. 19:18).
See 6:4. Something that is fleeting and insubstantial.

See note on 12:9.

**you know no God but me.** This statement contrasts with the idolatry of v. 2. The statement, reminding Israel that the covenant relationship is exclusive, is cast in the language of the first commandment (Ex. 20:2, 3; Deut. 5:6, 7) and adds the idea of “knowing” God. Other so-called gods are worshiped, but only the one true God can be “known” (Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes). Further linkage to the covenant requirements of the Decalogue is evident in the description of Israel’s idolatry (vv. 1, 2), a clear violation of the second commandment (Ex. 20:4–6; Deut. 5:8–10).

Israel is represented in corporate solidarity by the Hb. singular word for “you.” This form of the pronoun emphasizes the personal nature of God’s covenant relationship with His people. See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes; note on Gen. 17:7.

**wilderness.** During the difficult wilderness wanderings, God knew His people and was preparing them. Similarly, God will use the “wilderness” of exile to reclaim Israel (2:14–16).

Describes a step-by-step process of descent in morals and worship (Deut. 32:10–18; Jer. 2) due to material prosperity and self-reliance.

**forgot.** This pitiful climax stands in sharp contrast to the former days of knowledge (cf. vv. 4, 5 and notes; cf. Deut. 8:11–20).

This startling comparison of God to ferocious wild beasts that devour the flock echoes the covenant curses for disobedience (Lev. 26:21, 22; Deut. 32:24; Ezek. 14:21). These images depict the severity of divine judgment (5:14; cf. Prov. 17:12; Jer. 5:6; Lam 3:1–18).

Israel’s destruction is explained here in terms of the nation’s rebellion against her Divine Helper. There is no help like God (Ex. 18:4; Deut. 33:26–29; Ps. 10:14; 54:4; 115:9–11; 121:2–8; 146:5). To oppose Him is to invite destruction.

On Israel’s request for a monarchy, see 1 Sam. 8. On that occasion, the people’s asking for a king meant that they had rejected God as King (1 Sam. 13:9, 10). Their sense of security in having a king was a delusion.

Though describing past action, the Hb. verb tense suggests an ongoing process of giving and taking. The king is not specified. Perhaps this is a reference to the royal assassinations of Hosea’s time (3:4; 7:7; 8:4; 10:3; cf. 2 Kin. 15:8–31; 17:1–6), to an early king such as Saul (who was alive when kingship was first requested), or even to all of the kings of the north (all twenty of whom “did what was evil in the sight of the Lord”).

Lest they be diminished or forgotten, transgressions are figuratively tied up and then stored in a safe place for future retribution (7:2; 9:9; cf. Deut. 32:34, 35; Job 14:17).

**Ephraim.** See note on 4:17.

The predicament of Israel facing certain judgment is vividly compared to that of a mother and child during an unsuccessful birth (cf. 2 Kin. 19:3). This complex word picture compares Israel both to the mother (who faces sorrow and certain death) and to the child (who stubbornly refuses to be safely delivered).

**an unwise son.** Israel is depicted as a fetus that fails to position itself properly in the womb for delivery. This surprising figure relates to the theme of failure to acknowledge God.

verse_quote: Compassion is hidden from my eyes.
note: The Hb. for “pity” can have the sense of “repentance” or “regret.” God will not “repent” (i.e., change His mind) of His intention to vanquish death for His people. Paul quotes part of this verse in 1 Cor. 15:55.

Refers to Ephraim, whose name is from the same Hb. root as “fruitful” (9:16 note).

**east ... wind of the Lord.** Cf. 12:1 and note. Here this destructive force is a symbol for Assyria as God’s weapon of judgment against Israel (Introduction: Occasion; Is. 10:5, 6).

The capital city and driving force behind the northern kingdom’s rebellion.

**fall ... dashed ... ripped.** Figurative language for destruction (vv. 3, 8, 15) here gives way to chilling expressions of hard reality.

The prophet speaks to the people, urging repentance, before conveying God’s promise of blessing (vv. 4–8).

**14:1 Return.** This thematic exhortation to return (2:7; 3:5; 6:1; 7:10; 12:6) is now addressed to those who have already fallen because of their sins.

Words of confession accompanied by obedience please God, not half-hearted sacrifices (5:6; 6:6; 8:11–13). A precise wording for confession is suggested in vv. 2, 3.

**the vows of our lips.** Or, “fruit of our lips” (text note). The Hb. words for “bull calves” (here rendered “vows”) and “fruit” are similar. Cf. Prov. 12:14; 13:2; Heb. 13:15.

Israel is to give up trusting in foreign political powers (5:13; 7:11; 12:1), in her own military strength (10:13; cf. Ps. 33:16, 17), and in idolatrous and syncretistic religion (2:8, 13; 3:1; 4:12; 8:5, 6; 10:5, 6; 13:2).

**orphan finds mercy.** This expression alludes to the earlier theme of loss and restoration of love illustrated by Hosea’s marriage and his daughter, Lo-ruhama (1:6; 2:2–4, 14–23). See Introduction: Characteristics and Primary Themes.

The promise of healing begins to be realized when Israel returns from its sixth-century exile in Babylon. It finds much greater fulfillment in Jesus Christ and His church, and is consummated at His second coming.

**apostasy.** Israel’s characteristic unfaithfulness (4:10–12; 5:4; 7:4; 11:7) will be healed by the great Healer, whose anger is now turned away.

**love them freely.** In this love song, we hear again the deep affection of God for His elect. This undeserved love is what the NT calls grace (Rom. 5:15; Eph. 2:5, 8).

In this section, resplendent with the language of love, colorful metaphors drawn from plant life—a blossoming lily (Song 2:1, 16), a deeply rooted, sprouting and fragrant cedar of Lebanon (Pss. 92:12; 104:16), a splendid olive tree (Ps. 52:8; Jer. 11:16), a shade tree (Song 2:3; Ezek. 17:22, 23), flourishing grain (2:8, 22), a flowering vine (10:1; cf. Is. 5:1–7) and the fruit of the vine—depict a vigorous, renowned, stable, and prosperous Israel flourishing under God, who is likened to the life-giving dew (Deut. 33:13).
Like a tree renowned as a symbol of life (cf. Gen. 3:22; Rev. 22:2), God will give fruit to fruitless Ephraim (9:16 note).

This epilogue challenges every generation to consider carefully the ways of the Lord that are presented in the book (cf. Ps. 1; 18:21; Prov. 10:29). The choices that Israel—and every generation of God’s people—faces are also set before the reader: wisdom or folly; discipleship or rebellion; life or death. The wise will “choose life” (Deut. 30:19, 20).
